resources.string: The heaviest load you could probably lift once, estimated from a set of several reps.
Epley formula: load × (1 + reps ÷ 30), for every set. A session shows its best set. A single rep counts as the load itself. Example: 100 kg × 5 → 116.7 kg.

Completed working, drop and to-failure sets with a weight and at least one rep. Warm-ups, unfinished sets, unloaded or assisted bodyweight sets, bands and machines logged by plate number do not count.
It is an estimate, most accurate between 1 and 10 reps; it drifts with high reps and with sets far from failure. Use it to compare yourself over time, not as a real max.
The heaviest load you lifted for at least one rep in a session.
Maximum load among the session’s counted sets.
Completed working, drop and to-failure sets with a weight and at least one rep. Warm-ups do not count.
It ignores reps: 100 kg × 1 and 100 kg × 8 look the same. Check the estimated 1RM to take reps into account.
How much weight you moved: load times reps, added up.

Σ load × reps over completed working, drop and to-failure sets. Dumbbell exercises logged from a routine exercise marked as using both hands count twice (one dumbbell per hand); what counts is the setting when the session was logged, so later changes to the routine do not change past volume. The calendar, the session detail and the records use this same number. Shown in your unit (kg or lb).

Bodyweight exercises count only added load: unloaded and assisted sets add 0 volume (they still count as effective sets). Warm-ups, unfinished sets, bands and machines logged by plate number add nothing.
Volume favours heavy compound lifts and high reps; it does not measure effort. A dumbbell exercise added outside a routine counts the load as you entered it.
The number of sets that did real work.
Count of completed sets that are not warm-ups and have at least one rep, a duration or a distance.
Working, drop and to-failure sets of any exercise, including bodyweight, timed and cardio sets.
Haltera cannot know how hard a set was: an easy set counts the same as a set to failure. RPE, when you log it, is not used to filter sets.
Your bests for one exercise variant, and when you set them.

Heaviest load (for at least one rep) · best estimated 1RM · most reps at a load (more reps than ever done at that load or heavier) · best session volume. A record must beat every earlier session strictly; ties keep the first date.
Completed working sets of the selected variant: barbell, dumbbells and the other variants keep separate records. The first session of a variant is the starting point, not a record.
Records are recalculated from your log, so editing or deleting old sessions can change them. Bands and machines logged by plate number are left out.
How many personal records you set in the period.
Count of records (heaviest load, estimated 1RM, reps at a load, session volume) set by sessions in the period, each compared with your whole history before that session.
Every variant and every kind of record counts separately, so one session can set several.
Records come easily with a new exercise or after a break, so more records does not always mean more progress.
Finished sessions started in the period.
Count of sessions with a start date in the period and an end time.
Routine and free sessions, live or logged afterwards. A session still in progress does not count yet.
A ten-minute session counts the same as a two-hour one.
How long a session usually lasts, from start to finish.
Σ (end time − start time) ÷ number of finished sessions. The chart shows that average for each week.
Finished sessions of the period, by the day they started.
It is only as accurate as the recorded times: a session finished late, or logged with a guessed duration, moves it. Edit the session’s date and time to fix it.
Σ (end time − start time) of the finished sessions in the period.
Every finished session of the period, routine or free.
It includes rest between sets and anything else between start and finish.
Sessions in each block of 7 days. When the chart uses 4-week blocks (long histories), each bar is the block’s sessions ÷ 4.
Finished sessions, by the day they started; several sessions on one day all count.
Blocks are counted back from today, so they do not always start on a Monday.
A smoothed line that hides day-to-day noise.
Each point is the average of that entry and up to 6 entries before it (7 entries in total).
Every body-weight entry, whatever the day.
It counts entries, not days: with irregular weigh-ins it spans different lengths of time, and it reacts to real changes a few entries late.
How this period compares with the one just before it.

Change = this period − previous period. % = change ÷ previous × 100. The period is the last 28, 91 or 364 days ending today (today included); the previous period is the same number of days right before it, so both have the same length and the same weekdays.
▲ means higher and ▼ lower: the arrows only describe the direction, not whether it is good. All time has no previous period.
Without anything in the previous period there is no percentage. Today is not over, so the current period can still grow.
Sessions you logged compared with what your active routine plans.

Planned per week = training days of the cycle × 7 ÷ cycle length (one routine day per calendar day). Logged per week = sessions in the period ÷ weeks in the period. Adherence = logged ÷ planned × 100.
Every finished session counts, routine or free. It can go above 100 %.
It uses the routine that is active today for the whole period. A routine without rest days has no weekly plan (it is followed in order, whenever you train), so adherence is not shown for it.
Each square is a day; coloured squares are days you trained.
Darker means more effective sets that day. The training days shown are split into four equal groups (quartiles) by effective sets, so the colours adapt to your usual amount.
Finished sessions by the day they started; several sessions on one day add up. Columns are weeks from Monday (top) to Sunday.
Colours are relative to the days shown, not absolute amounts. Tap a day to see its numbers.
The average weekly change of your estimated 1RM over this variant’s history.
Least-squares line through each session’s estimated 1RM against its date; its slope × 7 gives kg (or lb) per week. R² (0–1) says how well a straight line fits: close to 1 is a steady trend.
Sessions with an estimated 1RM; it needs at least 3.
Few sessions, one very good or bad day, or a long break can swing it. Progress is rarely a straight line, so read it together with the chart.
How your sets of this variant are spread by repetitions.
Effective sets counted in five ranges: 1–5, 6–8, 9–12, 13–20 and 21 or more reps. Tap a bar to see its share.
Effective sets with reps of the selected variant. Timed and distance sets are left out.
The ranges only describe what you did; none is better than another.
One row per session of this variant, newest first.

Best set = the set with the highest estimated 1RM (ties go to the heavier). e1RM = Epley estimate of that set. Volume = Σ load × reps. Δ = change of the estimated 1RM against the previous session that had one.
Completed working, drop and to-failure sets of the selected variant. PR marks a session that set at least one personal record.
It reads up to your last 200 sessions of the exercise.
Effective sets per week for each muscle group, this period against the previous one.
Effective sets of the exercises whose primary muscles include the group ÷ weeks in the period.

Primary muscles only, each in full: a set of an exercise with two primary muscles counts once for each. Secondary muscles are not counted. The routine analysis also adds half a set for secondary muscles, so its totals are higher; its direct part is what is counted here.
Muscles come from the exercise catalogue, a simplification of how exercises really load them.
Volume (load × reps) per week for each muscle group.
Σ load × reps of the exercises whose primary muscles include the group ÷ weeks in the period.
The usual volume rules (bodyweight adds only extra load) with primary muscles counted in full.
Volumes of different muscles are not comparable: legs move far more weight than arms.
How your effective sets split between opposite groups.

Ratio = weekly sets of the first side ÷ weekly sets of the second. Push: chest, shoulders, triceps. Pull: lats, middle back, biceps, traps. Upper body: chest, shoulders, arms, back, traps, neck. Lower body: quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, calves, adductors, abductors.
Effective sets by primary muscle. A set counts once per side even when several of its muscles are on that side. Abdominals, lower back and full-body exercises are left out.
A ratio only describes your split; there is no universally right value. Shoulders count as push, although rear-delt work is a pull.
Your average body weight in each calendar week.
Average = Σ entries of the week ÷ number of entries. Δ = this week’s average − the previous week with entries.
Weeks run Monday to Sunday; weeks without entries are skipped.
A week with a single entry is as noisy as that one weigh-in.
How much your latest entry differs from a month earlier.
Latest entry − the oldest entry within the 30 days before it.
Needs at least one earlier entry inside those 30 days.
It compares two single weigh-ins, so daily swings of water and food show in it. The rate of change uses every recent entry instead.
How fast your body weight has been changing per week lately.
Least-squares line through the entries of the last 28 days; its slope × 7 gives kg (or lb) per week.
Needs at least 3 entries spread over 7 days or more.
Water, food and the time of day move body weight by 1–2 kg; weighing in under similar conditions gives a cleaner trend.
Puts the estimated 1RM of another variant or exercise on the same chart.
Each line is the best estimated 1RM of each session of that variant, on the same scale.
The same rules as the estimated 1RM.
Different exercises have different strength levels: compare their shapes and trends more than their heights.
Connect Health Connect in Settings → Integrations to see your steps, calories, resting heart rate and sleep here. Nothing is read until you do.
Steps are switched off or not allowed in Health Connect. Turn them on in Settings → Integrations.
No steps in Health Connect yet. A phone or a watch that counts steps fills this chart.
From Health Connect; the dashed line is your goal
Monday to Sunday; this week so far
kcal per day, as Health Connect reports them
How many steps Health Connect counted on each day, against your daily goal.

Health Connect adds up the steps of every app and device for each local day (midnight to midnight in your time zone) and removes overlaps by your priority order. Haltera shows that total; the dashed line is your goal (8 000 unless you change it).
Steps written to Health Connect by your phone, watch or other apps. A day with no data is shown empty, not as zero.
Only as accurate as the device that counts them; steps can arrive hours later from a watch. Haltera reads the last 30 days when you connect and keeps adding new days.
Sum of the steps of the 7 days before today ÷ the number of those days that have data.
Complete days only: today is still in progress and is left out. Days without data are skipped, not counted as zero.
A week with few days of data (the phone left at home) can look higher or lower than it was.
The day with the most steps in the period shown.
Highest daily total in the period; on a tie, the most recent day.
Every day of the period with data, today included.
One unusual day (a hike, a duplicated source) can stand out a lot.
How many days in a row you reached your steps goal.
Counts back day by day from yesterday while each day reached the goal; today is added once it reaches the goal. The longest streak is the longest such run in the days read.
Days at or above the goal. A day without data ends the streak.
Changing the goal changes past streaks too. Only the days copied from Health Connect (from 30 days before connecting) are considered.
Total steps of each calendar week and the average per day.
Total = sum of the daily totals from Monday to Sunday. Per day = total ÷ days of that week with data.
The current week counts the days so far.
Weeks with missing days have a smaller total; compare the per-day average instead.
Active and total energy burned per day, as other apps reported it to Health Connect.
Health Connect sums the active calories and the total calories of each local day. Haltera does not calculate them.
Total includes the resting energy your devices or apps estimate; active is the part from movement and exercise.
Wearables and apps estimate energy with large errors (often 20 % or more). Use it to see trends, not exact numbers.
The daily resting heart rate recorded by your watch or another app.
Average of the resting heart rate values Health Connect has for each local day. The subtitle is the mean of the 7 days before today with data.
Only resting heart rate values, not heart rate during exercise.
Shown as a trend only. It varies with sleep, stress, illness, caffeine and the device. This is a logbook, not a medical measurement.
How long you slept each night, as your watch or sleep app recorded it.
Sum of the sleep recorded from 18:00 the day before to 18:00 on each date, so a night counts for the morning it ended. The subtitle is the mean of the 7 nights before today with data.
Sleep sessions written to Health Connect, naps before 18:00 included.
Shown as a trend only. Trackers estimate sleep and often miss or add time awake.
Log a measurement (waist, arm, body fat or one you name) to see how it changes.
Log another entry within 30 days to see the change.
Log two entries to draw the line.
Enter a value above 0 and up to %1$s.
How much your latest entry of this measurement differs from a month earlier.
Latest entry − the oldest entry of the same measurement within the 30 days before it.
Needs at least one earlier entry of the same measurement inside those 30 days. Measurements you named alike (ignoring capitals and spaces) count as one.

It compares two single measurements, so where and how tight the tape sits shows in it. Body fat estimates from scales, calipers or photos differ a lot between methods: compare entries taken the same way.
Add progress photos to see how you change over time.
Photos stay on this device only: they are never uploaded, backed up or exported. Deleting the app deletes them.
Adding photos is not available on this device yet.
It is removed from this device for good.
That photo could not be read. Try another one.
The photo could not be saved. Check the free space and try again.
